title: Words that build
hook: Group chats, gossip, little lies to get through the day. Your tongue is where character shows first.

screens.text: You can pray five times a day and still wreck someone with one sentence. Today is about the most-used part of your body: your mouth (and your thumbs).
**One simple rule.** The Prophet ﷺ said: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should say something good or stay quiet [Bukhari 6018].

screens.title: Three filters before you speak, post or forward

steps.text: **Is it kind,** or at least fair?

screens.done_text: Fail one, and silence is usually the better deed.

screens.text: **Ghibah** (backbiting) is saying something about a person who isn't there that they'd hate to hear.
bubbles: The Companions asked: what if it's true? The Prophet ﷺ said that's exactly what backbiting is. If it's false, it's worse: slander [Muslim 2589].
The Qur'an compares backbiting to eating your dead brother's flesh, an image meant to make you recoil [Q 49:12].

screens.situation: In a masjid group chat, someone posts: "Saw Brother Dre at a bar downtown last night 👀 so much for the new convert." A few people react with laughing emojis.

options.text: Reply: "Let's not do this. Maybe there's a story we don't know." Then message Dre privately, kindly
options.feedback: Yes. You protect his honor in public and check on him in private. Maybe he was picking up a friend.

options.text: Say nothing and mute the chat
options.feedback: Better than joining in, but a short word of defense could end it. Silence can look like agreement.

options.text: Add a laughing emoji; you didn't say anything
options.feedback: Not quite. An emoji is a vote. It keeps the backbiting going.

options.text: Call the poster a hypocrite in the chat
options.feedback: Not quite. Right instinct, wrong tool. Shaming them publicly is the same mistake, aimed the other way.

cards.back: Being true is what makes it backbiting. If it were false, it'd be slander [Muslim 2589].

cards.front: Telling your mentor how a relative is hurting you, to get advice
cards.back: Seeking help with a real wrong is different from gossip [Q 4:148; Bukhari 5364]. Say only what's needed, to someone who can help.

cards.front: Warning a friend that a person online is scamming converts
cards.back: Protecting someone from real harm is allowed. Stick to the facts; skip the commentary.

cards.front: Sharing a viral clip about a Muslim speaker "just in case it's true"
cards.back: Check first. The Qur'an says to verify news before acting on it, or you may harm people [Q 49:6].

screens.text: **Honesty, all the way down.** Truthfulness leads to goodness, and lying leads to wrongdoing; a person who keeps choosing one becomes known for it [Bukhari 6094].
bubbles: That includes small lies: "tell them I'm in a meeting," a fake sick day, a padded excuse.
Honest doesn't mean harsh. You can be truthful *and* gentle: "I'd rather not say" is honest too.

options.text: Telling coworkers, while she's out, that Maria always messes up orders, which is true
options.feedback: Right. True, but she'd hate it said behind her back. That's what backbiting is.

options.text: Asking a mentor how to deal with a friend who keeps pressuring you
options.feedback: Not quite. Seeking help with a real problem is different from gossip.

options.text: Telling Maria privately that she missed an item, kindly
options.feedback: Not quite. Saying it to her, kindly, is advice, not backbiting.

screens.title: Already said it? Here's the repair

steps.text: Say something good about that person, especially where you said the bad.
Not sure whether to tell the person? Ask {{mentor.name}} first.

chips: Is venting to a friend about my boss backbiting?
How do I leave a gossip conversation without being awkward?
Are white lies okay to spare someone's feelings?
I backbit someone. Do I have to tell them?

screens.text: Try a 24-hour "say good or stay quiet" challenge.
steps: Run the three filters before you speak, post or forward
If a conversation turns to someone who isn't there, change the subject
Or say one good thing about them
screens.optional_extra: Think of someone you've talked about unfairly. Make du'a for them by name tonight.

screens.text: Say good or stay quiet. Backbiting is saying true things people would hate to hear behind their back; check news before you share it, and stay honest, gently.
One kinder sentence a day adds up to a different person.

check.prompt: What's the Prophet's rule ﷺ for speaking?

options.text: Say something good or stay quiet
options.feedback: Right. A rule for anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day [Bukhari 6018].

options.text: Say whatever's true, no matter what
options.feedback: Not quite. True things can still be backbiting. Say good or stay quiet [Bukhari 6018].

check.prompt: If what you say about an absent person is true, is it still backbiting?

options.text: Yes, if they'd hate to hear it
options.feedback: Right. True is backbiting; false is slander [Muslim 2589].

options.text: No, the truth is always fine to share
options.feedback: Not quite. Backbiting is exactly the true things they'd hate to hear [Muslim 2589].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Say good or stay silent [Bukhari 6018].
- Backbiting (ghibah) is mentioning an absent person in a way they'd dislike; if true, it's backbiting, if false, slander [Muslim 2589]. The Qur'an forbids it with the image of eating a dead brother's flesh, and also forbids suspicion and spying [Q 49:12].
- Verify news before acting on or spreading it [Q 49:6].
- Truthfulness leads to righteousness; lying leads to wrongdoing [Bukhari 6094].
- Speaking about a wrong done to you, to someone who can help, is allowed: Allah dislikes public mention of evil except by one who has been wronged [Q 4:148]; Hind described her husband's stinginess to the Prophet ﷺ to ask what she could do [Bukhari 5364]. Scholars extend this to asking advice and warning others of real harm, saying only what's needed. The tongue must be guarded from lying, slander and backbiting [Revealed Path ch. 15].
- Repairing backbiting: repent (tawbah), say good about the person where you spoke ill, make du'a for them. Whether to tell them and ask their pardon depends on the case; scholars weigh whether it would cause more harm. Route that to the mentor or imam.

**Likely questions**
- *"Is venting about my boss backbiting?"* Venting for its own sake usually is. Asking a trusted person for advice on how to handle the boss, with only the needed details, is different.
- *"How do I exit a gossip conversation?"* Light redirects: change the subject, say one good thing about the person, or "I'd rather not talk about them when they're not here."
- *"White lies?"* Keep the general picture: honesty is the default, and gentle honesty or saying nothing usually works. For specific situations (a spouse, reconciling people), scholars have detailed discussion; offer "Ask my imam" if they want a ruling.
- *"Do I have to tell the person I backbit them?"* Scholars weigh whether telling them would cause more hurt. Meanwhile: repent, say good about them, make du'a. Offer "Ask my imam" for their case.

**Escalate:** a conflict where they're being slandered or bullied at the masjid or online (mentor/imam); anything that sounds like harassment or threats (safety rule).

**Don't**
- Don't name or discuss real people the convert mentions in a negative way; steer back to what they can do.
- Don't make them anxious about every sentence; the aim is a habit.
